newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: PEACOCK COULD BE US AMBASSADOR
There's renewed speculation former federal Liberal leader, Andrew Peacock, will be appointed as Australia's next Ambassador to the United States.
The post becomes vacant early next year, following the appointment of the incumbent, John McCarthy, as Australia's new envoy to Indonesia.
Mr Peacock, who was Foreign Minister in the Fraser Government, has been pursuing business interests since resigning from Federal Parliament in 1994.
A spokesman for Foreign Minister, Alexander Downer, refused to comment on the speculation, saying an appointment will be made in due course.
UNION DECRIES ABC CUTS
The Community and Public Sector Union says Australian content on ABC television will fall to less than 30 percent by the year 2000 and whole radio networks will be axed, as a result of funding cuts.
ABC Managers yesterday told a Senate committee in Canberra that 900 positions are likely to be cut over the next two financial years because of Federal Government funding cuts.
That's just under 20 per-cent of the Corporation's current workforce.
CPSU officer, Lisa Fowkes, folks says people have to understand that jobs in the ABC translate directly into programming, and the cuts will mean a loss of localism.
JAPANESE JEOPARDISING TOURISM; OPERATOR
There's a claim that Australia's tourism reputation is being jeopardised by young Japanese people working in our tourism industry.
It comes from a Japanese tourism operator, Hiroshi Matsuda, who says young Japanese on working holiday visas often don't speak English or know enough about Australia to provide a quality service.
He told the Parliamentary Committee on Migration the number of visas issued for Japanese guides is excessive, and the working holiday scheme should be reevaluated to protect Australian jobs.
STATE LEADERS MEET TODAY
The Northern Territory Chief Minister will ask today's leaders' forum in Melbourne to tell the Federal goverment not to interfere in the rights of state and territory parliaments to make laws.

Shane Stone claims A-C-T Chief Minister Kate Carnell, and Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett have already agreed to join the Territory in opposing the Federal bill to over-ride the Territory's euthanasia law.
But New South Wales Premier, Bob Carr, regards it as a dispute between the Commonwealth and the Northern Territory.
Also at today's forum, Queensland and New South Wales will stress that the national gun buy-back scheme could be at risk unless the Federal Government provides more money to administer it.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
